scenarios.title: Tutorial: A Good Start with Leo
scenarios.topic: A friendly check-in: a strong reader whose reading log keeps coming back blank

prevalence.text: 33% of U.S. fourth graders performed at or above the NAEP Proficient level in reading in 2022.

why_address_it.text: "When schools, families, and community groups work together to support learning, children tend to do better in school, stay in school longer, and like school more."
why_address_it.source: Henderson & Mapp, A New Wave of Evidence (SEDL, 2002)

massachusetts.text: Massachusetts fourth graders' average NAEP reading score is consistently among the highest in the nation.

setting.meeting_context: A short, teacher-requested check-in after school on a Thursday in Room 108. Ms. Martins came straight from work and brought Leo with her.

scenarios.teacher_concern: Leo's weekly reading log has come back blank or half-filled for three of the last four weeks, so he's missing the reading-log points on his report card. You'd like to agree on a simple routine at home.
scenarios.student_strength: BUT I notice Leo is one of the most enthusiastic readers in the room. He's always the first to volunteer during read-aloud, and last week he explained the ending of our chapter book to his whole table.

A.title: Leo's Reading Progress
A.summary: Leo reads above grade level and his fall-to-winter reading level went up two steps. Reading-log points: 1 of 4 weeks complete this month.

B.title: Weekly Reading Log
B.summary: Leo's log for the last four weeks: week 1 is full, weeks 2 and 3 are blank, week 4 has two nights filled in. Parent signature lines are empty.

parent_persona.name: Sofia Martins
parent_persona.personality: Warm, friendly and a little apologetic. She works as a dental hygienist and evenings are busy with Leo and his baby sister. She's proud of Leo and wants to help. When she feels the teacher is on Leo's side, she's easy to talk to.
parent_persona.speaking_style: Friendly and chatty, laughs easily, says 'oh, I know' and 'that's so him'. Asks practical questions.
knows: Leo loves to read, especially comics and dragon books.
The reading log goes home in his folder, but she doesn't always see it.
Evenings are hectic since the baby was born in the summer.
She thinks Leo is doing well in school.
hiding: She never really understood the log was graded; she thought it was optional.
She's a little worried Leo will struggle like his older cousin did, and she'd love ideas for how to keep him reading.
parent_persona.likely_claim: Leo reads every night, she's sure of it; they just forget to write it down.
softens_when: The teacher says something nice and specific about Leo.
The teacher asks about their evenings.
The teacher suggests something simple and practical.
escalates_when: The teacher makes it sound like she doesn't care about Leo's reading.

student_persona.name: Leo Martins
student_persona.personality: Cheerful, talkative, a bit shy at first with grown-ups in a meeting. Lights up when books come up.
student_persona.speaking_style: Short, excited sentences. Says 'um' a lot. Loves to name the book he's reading.
knows: He reads comics in bed with a flashlight most nights.
The log is at the bottom of his backpack and he forgets about it.
He is reading a dragon series and is on book three.
hiding: He reads under the covers after lights-out and is afraid he'll get in trouble for staying up.
student_persona.likely_claim: He does read. He just forgets the paper.
speaks_up_when: The teacher asks him directly.
Someone mentions books, dragons, or read-aloud.

counselor.name: Grace Whitfield
counselor.title: School Counselor
counselor.knows: Knows Leo as a happy, well-adjusted kid. No concerns on file. Suggests praising the reading he already does and keeping any routine tiny.

nurse.name: Tom Aldana
nurse.title: School Nurse
nurse.knows: No health concerns on file for Leo. Mentions that eight-year-olds need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep, so a bedtime reading routine with a set lights-out can help.

principal.name: Janelle Ruiz
principal.title: Principal
principal.knows: The school counts reading minutes any way families can manage: a photo of the log, a quick note, or the class app. The log is meant to build a habit, not to punish.

colleague.name: Ben Castillo
colleague.title: Grade 3 teacher next door
colleague.knows: Has had luck letting students keep the log taped inside their book instead of in the folder, so it's there when they read.

scenarios.title: Chronic Absence: Maya
scenarios.topic: Student is repeatedly absent and missing content

prevalence.text: "The U.S. rate of chronic absenteeism ... decreased to 28% in the 2022-23 school year."

why_address_it.text: "Chronic absenteeism is the single strongest predictor of dropping out before graduation."

massachusetts.text: 17.1% of students were chronically absent in 2025-26, down from 22.2% in 2022-23.

setting.meeting_context: Attendance meeting after 5 unexcused absences, Tuesday December 2, 2025, 3:15 PM, Room 214. Ms. Reyes left work early to be here. Maya came with her.

scenarios.teacher_concern: Maya has missed 12 days this year (5 of them unexcused) and been tardy 6 times. She missed the Unit 3 quiz and homework and hasn't made them up, so her Algebra I grade is a 64 even though she averages 88% on in-class work. Your email and voicemail to her mom got no reply.
scenarios.student_strength: BUT I notice that when Maya is here, she aces the warm-up and the classwork (10/10, 18/20). She also told me she walks her little brother Jayden to school in the mornings.

A.title: Notice of Absences
A.summary: System-generated letter dated 11/21/25: Maya has 12 absences (5 unexcused) and 6 tardies this year. Under district policy the school will contact the family to schedule a meeting to develop attendance action steps together.

B.title: Gradebook Assignment Detail: Algebra I, Q1
B.summary: Warm-up week 6 (10/14) 10/10 and Unit 3 classwork (10/15) 18/20, both done in class. Unit 3 quiz (10/20): absent, not made up. Unit 3 homework (11/03): absent. In-class average 88%; overall 64%.

C.title: Parent Contact Log: Maya R.
C.summary: 10/21 emailed the missed-work list, no reply. 11/04 phone voicemail asking for a callback. 11/07 Maya said she walks her brother Jayden to school. 11/10 shared with the counselor for follow-up.

knows: Maya has been out "a few times" and she wrote notes saying Maya was sick.

student_persona.speaking_style: Short, flat teenage answers ('I guess', 'it's fine'). Longer and warmer when talking about math puzzles or Jayden. Never swears in front of her mom.
knows: She has missed more days than her mom realizes.
On some mornings she walks Jayden to Pemberton Falls Elementary and signs him in late, then skips school because she would be so late.
She falls behind on homework because she watches Jayden after school.

That the "sick" days were mostly Jayden days.

Her mom is being blamed or looks upset.
Someone mentions math, the warm-ups, or Jayden.

nurse.name: Patricia Lindqvist
nurse.title: School Nurse

principal.name: Dr. Renée Castellanos
principal.title: Principal

colleague.name: Holly Brandt
colleague.title: Grade 9 Biology teacher

B.title: Nurse Visit Log: Mateo L.
B.summary: Three visits: 09/18 cough and wheezing after recess (inhaler, back to class), 10/06 stomachache (rested 15 min, back to class), 10/14 cough (parent called, picked up early). Asthma action plan on file, updated 08/2026.

C.title: Kindergarten Progress Snapshot

D.title: Massachusetts Minimum School Age (603 CMR 8.02)
D.summary: Massachusetts requires attendance starting in September of the calendar year a child turns six. Mateo turns 6 in April 2027, so the law does not require him to attend yet; the conversation has to rest on why kindergarten attendance matters, not on compulsory attendance.

scenarios.title: Reading Below Benchmark: Elena
scenarios.topic: Second grader is well below benchmark on the fall literacy screener

prevalence.text: 40% of U.S. fourth graders performed below NAEP Basic in reading in 2024, the largest share since 2002.

why_address_it.text: Students who don't read proficiently by third grade are four times more likely to leave high school without a diploma than proficient readers.
why_address_it.source: Annie E. Casey Foundation, Double Jeopardy (2011)

massachusetts.text: Only 40% of MA students in grades 3-8 met or exceeded expectations in ELA on the 2026 MCAS, down 2 points from 2025 and 12 points from 2019.

setting.meeting_context: Teacher-requested follow-up on the fall literacy screener, Thursday October 22, 2026, 3:20 PM, Room 112. Mr. Vasquez came straight from the garage. Elena is with him.

scenarios.teacher_concern: Elena's fall literacy screener came back well below benchmark (14th percentile). Decoding and oral reading fluency are well below, and in guided reading she guesses words from the first letter. She started a Tier 2 phonics group on 10/05.
scenarios.student_strength: BUT I notice Elena has a rich vocabulary and predicted the ending of our read-aloud before anyone else. In math centers she explained her strategy to the whole group.

A.title: Fall Literacy Screener Family Report
A.summary: Grade 2, 09/22/26. Composite well below benchmark (14th percentile). Letter naming at benchmark; decoding (nonsense words) and oral reading fluency well below benchmark. Screening does not diagnose dyslexia or other disabilities.

B.title: Anecdotal Record: Elena V.
B.summary: 09/24 read-aloud: rich vocabulary, predicted the ending. 09/29 guided reading: guessed words from the first letter. 10/01 partner reading: asked to "just listen" instead of read. 10/06 math centers: explained her strategy to the group.

C.title: Tier 2 Reading Intervention Plan
C.summary: Started 10/05/26: phonics small group, 4 x 30 min a week with Ms. Okafor, focused on short vowels and consonant blends, progress checked every 2 weeks. 10/19 check: decoding up from 11 to 17 words correct.

D.title: Massachusetts Early Literacy Screening (603 CMR 28.03(1)(f))
D.summary: Within 30 school days of a screening result significantly below benchmark, the school must tell the parent the results and the school's response and offer a follow-up discussion. This conference is that required follow-up.

E.title: Spring Grade 1 Screener Follow-Up
E.summary: Elena's spring Grade 1 screener (05/2026) was already below benchmark (22nd percentile). The family results letter sat as a draft and was never sent, and the Tier 2 recommendation for fall was never carried over to the Grade 2 roster. The family was never told.

delivery.subject: Elena V., spring Grade 1 screener
delivery.body: Flagging this before your meeting. Elena was already below benchmark last spring, but her results letter never went home and her Tier 2 recommendation fell off the roster over the summer. That one is on us.
